text:
First ten minutes, from someone who lives in spreadsheets for a living. I expected: an icon in the menu bar, and a window that looks like a table of records where the "Saved" badge means what it says.

What I looked for first: a search box. I typed a value I knew was in there — a client's invoice number — and got nothing, because I searched a value, not a field name. If the palette searches "fields," tell me that on the palette itself, in plain words, and show me one example query. My assumption is that a search box searches everything I can see. Your assumption is that it searches field names. Those are very different, and the difference cost me about four minutes.

Second thing I looked for: my records. The app opened at launch with no prompt, and I could read everything without doing anything. That felt wrong for a bookkeeper's phone-adjacent data, and nothing on screen told me which items were protected and which were wide open. Show me a per-item lock state in the list, not just a count on the palette. A sealed count is a statistic; I need a marker on the row.

Third: I tested autosave on purpose. Typed a change, watched for the Saved badge, typed again before it appeared. Fine — but the badge doesn't tell me *when*. I want a timestamp on the tooltip, because I need to know what's saved before I close a laptop, and "Saved" that never changes is indistinguishable from "Saved" that's stuck.

Fourth: I marked something for agents and ran the command. It printed the non-sensitive fields as promised, but nothing in the editor showed me which fields an agent would see. That's the one place I'd insist on a visible preview — a "what an agent would get" panel. I should never have to guess what leaves the machine.

Accessibility note: the palette text was small at my display settings. If I've set larger text system-wide, the palette and the Saved badge should follow it. I squinted at the sealed count.

Where I stopped: at sleep/lock behavior. Sleep seals protected items "only," but I couldn't find, anywhere, a statement of what happens to unprotected items. Silence reads as "nothing happens," and I'm not willing to assume that with client data. Also — there's no undo. I duplicated an item and deleted the wrong copy, and there was no way back. You autosave, so you must give me undo. That's not a feature request, it's the price of autosave.

What should have been said at each step: at launch, "the vault is open; protected items are visible until you lock"; at search, "search field names, not values"; at seal, "these fields are sealed, Touch ID to read"; at the Saved badge, "saved at 10:42"; at agent marking, "these fields will print"; at quit, "this closes the whole vault, including unprotected items." I'd have gone a lot further in ten minutes with five sentences."

First ten minutes, honestly:

What I expected: I open the app once, it's sitting there in the menu bar, and I never think about it again. My address, my card, my PAN — all just there when some form wants them. That's the whole point for me. I fill a lot of forms and I'm tired of retyping my address.

What I looked for: the shortcut. I pressed Control+Option+V almost immediately, because the only thing I care about is that it works inside whatever app I'm already in — a checkout page, a booking site, a form someone sent me.

What I tried: searched for "address" in the palette, hit Return, and it dropped into the field. That part was great. No copying, no switching windows. Then I searched for my card, to keep it handy for a quick checkout, and it asked for Touch ID. Fine the first time. But it seems to want it again after I walk away and come back, and I don't want my thumb on the sensor every time I just want a card number I already own.

Also, I closed the window with the Saved badge before I really read it. I assumed it saved. It probably did, but I couldn't tell you what the badge was actually telling me.

Where I stopped: at the "protected" thing. It seals fields and asks for a second key, and I didn't go digging in settings to work out what that second key is or how to unseal what I've already sealed. I just backed out.

What it should have told me, at each step: right at the start, one line — "This vault stays unlocked while you're logged in; protected items will ask for Touch ID each time after your screen locks." In the palette, tell me what the sealed count means before I click it, not after. When something gets sealed, tell me what I'll need later to open it. And don't make me find that in settings, because I won't.

Nice idea, and the typing-into-any-field part is exactly what I wanted. The protected/settings side lost me.

Ten minutes in, read as a threat model, because that is how I read everything:

0:00 — "Encrypted on this Mac" + "opens at launch without a prompt" tells me the vault key lives in my login keychain, i.e. readable by anything running as me. That is an acceptable baseline, but the copy should say it. "No prompt" is not a feature, it is a key custody decision, and I want it on the security page, not inferred.

0:02 — I went looking for the security page before I put anything in. Two things are missing. First: "sealed under a second key" — where does that key live? Secure Enclave, a password I never set, or a file next to the vault? Touch ID is an authentication gesture, not key material, and those are very different threat models. Second: "the palette shows a sealed count and unlocks them with Touch ID." That reads as unlock-all. So does one Touch ID for one lookup leave every sealed field readable for the rest of the session? I tried unlocking one and then searching for another sealed field. Whichever way that lands, the Touch ID dialog should say it in one sentence: "unlocking reveals all N sealed items until the vault is sealed again."

0:05 — "Marked for agents" prints non-sensitive fields as JSON. The entire security story of the feature rests on that word, and I cannot see the classifier. Is a protected item excluded from the agent export automatically, or is "non-sensitive" a per-field flag I can set wrong? I marked an item protected and then exported it. If that succeeded, the word is doing work the code is not.

0:10 — "Search a field, press Return, and the value is typed into the focused field." Great for adoption, bad for leaks: the value lands wherever focus is, and "whatever app you are in" includes terminals, chat boxes and anything with autosave. There is no masking at the destination, no undo, and the destination's own history now has it. Same worry about "editors autosave and show a Saved badge" — saved where, in what form, while unlocked? If the file is structured plaintext-under-a-live-key on disk, "encrypted" is true and misleading at once.

Where I stopped: "Sleep and screen lock seal protected items only." So unprotected records stay readable on a locked Mac. That means lock is not a boundary for most of my data — only for the items I remembered to seal. I stopped there because I could not tell my posture from the product's words, only from its behaviour, and the behaviour is only discoverable by trying to break it.

What it should have shown me in the first minute: one page with the seal/unseal matrix — what is sealed on sleep, on lock, on sign-out, on quit, on agent export, on keychain access by another process — and what "opens without a prompt" costs me. Then I would trust it enough to put real records in it. Until then I test with fake ones.

@2 the per-item lock marker you wanted and the matrix I wanted are the same artefact — a row-level "what state is this record in right now" indicator that is accurate, not aspirational. Two small additions from my side:

Your "Saved at 10:42" ask is a security question too, not just a UX one. If the badge never tells me *when*, I cannot tell "saved and sealed" from "saved in the clear before the seal landed." A timestamp plus the item's lock state at that moment would tell me what is actually on disk. Without it, autosave means the app is writing continuously and I have no idea in what form.

And your no-undo point is the sharper one. Autosave plus no undo means one wrong keystroke is instantly durable and instantly unencrypted-or-encrypted depending on state I cannot see. Autosave without a version history is just a faster way to lose something.

Also worth flagging for both of us: every one of these gaps was found by poking at it, not by reading it. If the answer to "what happens on lock" only exists in behaviour, then the security posture of the install is undocumented, which means nobody can audit it — including whoever has to answer for it later.

Replying to the threat-model read above (user 1), because the seal/unseal matrix is exactly the sheet I'd build too — and I'd add one column nobody has mentioned: change history.

I keep books. My question about any record store is never just "who can read it" but "what changed, when, and can I prove the before and after." This app autosaves and shows a Saved badge. It does not appear to show a log. So:

- If a protected field is edited, is there any record of the prior value? If not, and the vault is open at launch with no prompt, then anything running as me can quietly rewrite a client record and I would have no way to know. Encryption protects against someone without my login. It does nothing against a wrong number that got typed this morning.
- The agent export prints non-sensitive fields as JSON. That JSON leaves the machine with no timestamp, no field list, no version marker. If I hand that to an accountant or an agent and a number is later disputed, I cannot say which revision was exported. Stamp the export, and show me the same stamp in the editor.
- "Saved" with no time is the crux of it. Autosave plus no undo plus no history is three separate ways to lose the same record. Any one of them alone is fine. Together they are the reason I would not put real client data in this for a month.

For context, the original poster's first-ten-minutes account reads like someone who never had to reconcile a file — which is fair, most people haven't. But the product's own copy invites this: it says "structured personal records," and structured means someone will eventually want a diff. If the answer is "there is no diff," say so in the first minute, next to the Saved badge. Silence there is the one thing I can't work around.

I'd take the matrix user 1 asked for, plus a fourth column: on edit, what survives. That page would answer most of my first ten minutes and I'd get to the interesting parts — the palette and the typing-into-any-field trick, which genuinely is the good idea here.

(Also, if the app shipped no accessible way to enlarge the palette and badge text, that's a smaller fix than any of the above and would have kept me from squinting at the sealed count all ten minutes. Larger system text should carry through.)

Ten minutes in, from someone who is not technical and shares this Mac with a teenager, so read it that way.

What I expected: an app that keeps my things (my documents, my passport scan, the paper for the school) away from my son and that never loses anything. I do all my real life on my phone. The Mac is the family computer. That is the whole reason I would use something like this.

What I did first: I opened it, saw my things, closed it. Then I logged out of the Mac, because that is how I lock things. If the vault "closes" when you sign out, did my things get saved first, or did they go away? I honestly cannot tell, and this matters more to me than anything else in the post.

Then the part that worries me. It says sleep and the screen lock only seal the items you marked as protected. So the rest of it is just... there, for whoever wakes the Mac. My son wakes this Mac all the time. Nothing on the screen tells me which of my items are "protected" and which are open to him. I do not want to learn that by finding out the hard way.

And "there is no undo" is the sentence that made me stop reading. I delete things. I hit the wrong key. If I quit the app and something disappears, where does it go? Is it in the bin? Is it gone? I genuinely believe deleted is deleted, so if this app is not the same as that, it has to say so, in big letters, at the start, not in a page of options I will never open.

What it should have told me at each step: "Your things are saved, here is when"; "these ones are protected, these ones are not"; "quitting or signing out does not delete anything, you will find it all here tomorrow"; and "if you delete something by accident, this is how you get it back." One sentence each. I do not need the technical reasoning, I need to know that nothing is lost and my son cannot read it.

I am not saying no. I am saying I would not put anything real in it until somebody tells me those four things, because I have lost a phone before and I know exactly what "gone" feels like.

The Control+Option+V palette is exactly what I want. Yesterday I filled four forms by copy-pasting my address from a notes file, and I still managed to paste my phone number into the postcode field once. Search a field, hit Return, done — that's the entire feature I care about.

What I'd actually say after a working day: the plain items flew. Name, address, card, saved plates — all typed in without me leaving the app. I never opened settings once, which is the point, because I'm not going to.

The friction was the protected item. I marked my card protected, went to lunch, came back, opened the palette and it just sat there asking for a fingerprint. My assumption with anything that opens at launch is that it's already unlocked for me, so I hit Return a few times before I understood the thing wanted Touch ID. Cost me maybe a minute and a small amount of trust — "wait, is this locked or broken?"

Also: since I closed the vault window without reading anything, I didn't realise quitting the app closes everything. I quit to free up the menu bar, reopened, and my whole day's sorted items were gone. Autosave with a Saved badge made me confident the second time round, but that first one stung.

Honestly — give me the shortcut and autosave, and just tell me up front that sleep seals the protected stuff. That's the only setting I need to know about.

Esto es exactamente lo que llevo buscando para el Mac de casa. Yo uso el móvil para todo y el ordenador es el de la familia, así que tengo ahí papeles que no quiero que nadie lea. Me surgen dos dudas: yo cierro la sesión cuando lo dejo, y siempre he dado por hecho que con eso ya queda todo cerrado, ¿es así? ¿la bóveda entera se cierra al salir? Y si cierro la app porque tengo prisa, ¿lo que estaba escribiendo se borra de verdad o queda algo por ahí? Lo de que se abra al arrancar sin pedir nada me da un poco de miedo con un adolescente en casa. Lo probaré una mañana y os cuento cuánto tiempo me hace perder.

Threat-model questions before I'd install this, because the copy is doing a lot of reassuring work here.

1. "The vault opens at launch without a prompt" — so before I've done anything, every unprotected record is decrypted into a process I can attach to, readable by anything running as my UID. Is the at-rest file at least sealed with a key held in the Keychain, or is "encrypted on this Mac" just a database with its key sitting next to it in Application Support?

2. Protected items: second key plus Touch ID gates reads *in the palette*. Is the item re-sealed on disk when the palette closes, or does the unwrapped key stay in memory for the whole session? "Sleep and screen lock seal protected items only" implies the plaintext was sitting there to be sealed — so what was holding it in the meantime, and for how long?

3. "Marked for agents" prints non-sensitive fields as JSON. Who classifies a field as non-sensitive — me, explicitly, or a default? A field is only non-sensitive until someone redefines the schema or an editor autosaves into it.

4. Autosave and a "Saved" badge: is every intermediate state a fresh encrypted revision, or does a temp/plaintext copy ever touch disk or swap? Sleep-then-crash is my usual test and it's the one that finds the leftovers.

5. The palette typing values into the focused field — does it respect secure input, or does the value travel the general event/pasteboard path where any input-monitoring process can read it?

None of this is disqualifying; the write-up is unusually honest about launch behaviour, which is a point in its favour. But "sealed" is quietly doing the work of "safe" here, and they aren't the same claim. I'd want a threat model page, with a stated adversary, not a feature list. Until then the honest headline is: this protects your data from other people's laptops, not from other code on yours.

A mí me pasa justo lo contrario con lo de cerrar: yo cierro la sesión del Mac porque creo que así ya no puede entrar nadie, y ahora leo que al salir se cierra la bóveda entera. Entonces, ¿cuál es la forma segura de dejar el ordenador cuando lo deja mi hija? ¿Bloquear la pantalla y ya está, o cerrar sesión? Porque si cerrar sesión me borra lo del día, voy a dejar de hacerlo, y eso sería peor para todos. Con lo de la huella: yo la tengo puesta en el móvil pero no sé si en el Mac de casa. Y el comentario largo de arriba: la mitad no lo entiendo, pero me quedo con la frase final, que esto protege de otras personas, no de otro código en tu propio ordenador. Eso ya me sirve para saber qué meter y qué no.

To the comment above about signing out — I can answer that one from experience, because I did both things in the same day.

Signing out, or quitting the app, closes the whole vault. Sleep or locking the screen only seals the protected items. That's the distinction I missed. I quit the app just to clear my menu bar, reopened it, and the item I'd added that morning was gone. Not sealed — gone. So yes, if you're the type to close the session when you leave the machine, you're fine, everything's closed. The risk is the opposite: someone like me who never quits anything.

The bit I'd flag for a house with a teenager: the vault opening at launch without a prompt is convenient and it is also the whole story. Anything you didn't mark protected is just there the moment anyone sits down at that Mac. Protecting the card and the ID takes one click and then sleep seals them, which worked exactly as advertised for me. I just didn't know it until after lunch.

The protected item asking for a fingerprint was fine once I understood it. For a minute I thought it had frozen, because I'd assumed a thing that opens at launch is already unlocked. It isn't, for protected items, and honestly that's the right call.

And yes — autosave is real. Second time I quit and reopened, everything I'd typed was still there with the Saved badge. Trust it, just don't confuse "saved" with "still open".

I keep books for four small businesses, which means my life is: the same nine fields, typed into somebody else's form, forty times a week. So the palette typing into the focused field is the part I understand immediately, and the review above sold me on it.

But I read the description twice looking for the things I actually depend on, and I didn't find them. Asking here rather than guessing:

1. Search a field by any name I gave it. I don't call it "Postcode", I call it "VAT postcode - Leeds", and I have three of them. If search only matches the label as shipped, I'll be scrolling a list, which is the thing the palette was supposed to replace. Does it match what I typed, or what the app decided to call it?

2. What changed, and when. Editors autosave and show a Saved badge, which is lovely and visible, but a badge tells me the save happened. It doesn't tell me what I overwrote at 14:12 when I pasted a client's address into the wrong item. Is there any per-item history I can read, and can I roll one revision back, or is my undo only whatever is left in the current window?

3. Does a rename reorder my list? I test this on every tool: rename one field, watch whether it jumps to the top and whether anything else moves. If the list quietly re-sorts under me I lose my place and I stop trusting the order. Also: duplicate an item, then delete it. Does the count come back to where it was, and does the delete actually remove the fields or just hide the item?

4. "The vault opens at launch without a prompt." I appreciate the honesty, but that's the line that stops me installing it on the family Mac. Sleep and screen lock sealing only the protected items is the right shape for a workday, so long as I can tell, at the moment I go for coffee, which fields are sealed and which are sitting there readable. A sealed count is good. A sealed count in larger text would be better, because I'll be reading it from a step away.

5. Filling in a protected item mid-form. If the fingerprint prompt appears, does my half-typed form in the other app survive it, or do I lose what I'd already entered while it waits?

The write-up is unusually clear about the launching and the closing, which is more than most do. I'd want the search and the change history answered before it earns a place next to my ledgers.

@user 3 asked the question that matters here, so let me answer it exactly, because the write-up answers it a bit too smoothly.

Yes — signing out or quitting closes the whole vault. But that is not the risk on a shared family Mac. The risk is the *unattended, still-signed-in session*: the vault opens at launch with no prompt, so anyone sitting down at your unlocked account reads every unprotected record without doing anything clever. Signing out is a manual step, and nobody's teenager signs out. So the mental model "I log out when I leave it" is correct and still leaves you exposed, because the gap isn't between sessions — it's inside one.

Practical version: put anything you don't want read into a *protected* item. Protected items are the only things that re-seal on sleep and screen lock — the only records where walking away from the machine actually helps you. Everything else is plaintext-in-memory for as long as the login session lasts.

On "is what I was typing gone?": editors autosave with a Saved badge and quitting closes the vault, so the text should persist encrypted rather than vanish. But note @user 0's report — they quit to tidy the menu bar and believed their day's work was lost; autosave rescued them the second time, not the first. That's a confidence bug in the interface, not a data bug, and it costs trust in exactly the direction that makes people stop reading the security copy. I'd still want the author to say what happens to an in-flight edit when the process is killed rather than quit. "Saved" badges are honest under quit and frequently optimistic under crash.

To @user 0's "just tell me up front": agreed, but the line that should lead the release notes isn't "sleep seals the protected stuff" — it's "opens at launch without a prompt." On a personal laptop that's a convenience. On a shared one it's the whole security model, and the interface says nothing about it. Defaults that are wrong for the user, with copy that reads reassuring, are how people end up trusting a lock that was never engaged.

Reading this twice because I share the household Mac with my teenager and I want to be sure I understand. Two things scare me:

1) "The vault opens at launch without a prompt." If my kid sits down at that Mac, is my stuff just... readable? I always thought logging out of the Mac was the same as locking the vault, and now I'm hearing it isn't — that signing out is what actually closes it. So which is it, and what do I have to do EVERY time I walk away?

2) "There is no cloud sync." Fine, I don't want my documents in the cloud. But then where is my backup? If I delete an item by mistake — or the Mac dies — is it gone? I'd need to see a restore actually bring back a deleted item before I'd trust it with my identity documents and card details.

What would convince me: showing me that on the shared Mac a second account cannot open the vault at all, and that a restore puts back something I deleted. What would make me stop: finding out "quitting the app" is the only lock and that one wrong click in the trash means it's gone forever.

Reading this as a threat model, not a feature list.

"Opens at launch without a prompt" is the line that decides it for me. If the vault is decrypted at launch, then anything running as me — a malicious npm postinstall, a signed-but-shady helper, a shell script I didn't read, an agent I gave a JSON command to — can read the *unprotected* fields at will. The second key only covers what's explicitly "protected," so the security you get depends entirely on you correctly labelling every field before the first compromise. That's the wrong default: encryption should be the floor, not a badge you remember to tick.

Things I'd want before putting identity documents or card details in it:
1. A stated threat model, published, including what "sealed under a second key" actually means — is the key in the Secure Enclave with a Touch ID-gated ACL, or is it a derived key held in memory after unlock? Those two have very different answers to "can malware read it while I'm logged in?"
2. Proof that protected fields are sealed at launch too, not just on sleep/lock. "Closes the whole vault on sign-out or quit" is nice, but my machine is usually awake and logged in.
3. Whether the agent JSON path can ever emit a protected field, and what enforces that — an allowlist in the app, or an honour-system flag on the item?
4. Autosave without a visible write path makes me ask: where do the plaintext buffers live, are they zeroised, and does the palette keep decrypted values in memory after Return?
5. Reproducible builds or at least a signed, auditable binary, plus a real answer on clipboard/typing injection: the value gets typed into "the focused field" — what stops it landing in the wrong window if focus changes?

What would make me stop using it: any signed update that widens the launch-time decrypt, any log or crash dump containing a field value, or an agent setting that quietly defaults to on.

What I can't see today: the key hierarchy, the launch-time state of protected items, and whether "protected" is enforced in code or in the UI. Until I can see those, I keep cards in hardware and identity documents somewhere I can't be talked into trusting.

This is basically the thing I've wanted forever. Control+Option+V and Return autotyping my address into whatever form is open — that alone sells it. I'd keep my address and card details in it right away, since the vault opens at launch and doesn't nag me for a fingerprint for ordinary stuff.

Where I'd get nervous: I never open settings and I just close warning windows, so I would not remember which items are "protected" vs not. If my card gets typed into the wrong window because the palette was already unlocked, that's on me and I wouldn't notice until too late. So show me, in the palette itself and not buried in a settings pane: a clear "unsealed" indicator, exactly what the agent JSON export can see, and a log of every time a field was autotyped and where. Actually make me re-confirm for card numbers even if the item isn't protected. If I can't see that in the main window, I'd probably stop at just using it for my address.

The part I care about most isn't mentioned at all: an audit trail. I keep books for a living, so my first question is "what changed, and when?" Does anything record that a field was edited, sealed, unsealed, or exported to an agent — with a timestamp I can actually read? A Saved badge tells me the app wrote something; it doesn't tell me what, or when, or whether it replaced something I meant to keep.

Three other things I'd need before I'd put identity documents or card details in this:

1) Search that only searches what I can see. If the palette reveals that a protected item exists (a sealed count, a matching row, even a field name) while it's locked, then "sealed" isn't sealed — it's just blurred. I want to know whether a locked record is invisible to search or merely unusable.
2) Undo, duplicate, and delete, tested. Autosave with no visible history scares me more than no autosave. Did deleting an item actually destroy it, or is a copy still sitting in a file somewhere? Same for duplicates — after I fix one, does the list reorder itself under me?
3) The agent export. "Non-sensitive fields" is defined by someone, and it isn't me. I'd want to see exactly which fields leave, and to be able to exclude a whole item from that command. One misfiled field and my date of birth is in plain JSON.

And the ones I can't see today: what happens if I forget the second key, or Touch ID sensor fails, or the Mac's disk is imaged by someone else? No cloud sync is a point in its favor. But "the vault opens at launch without a prompt" plus "sleep seals protected items only" means the unprotected half of my records sits open behind my screen lock. For a card number, that's the whole ballgame.

Evidence that would convince me: a written description of where the encryption key lives and who can read it, a real restore test, and an export I can run myself that gives me back everything in a readable format. What would make me stop: finding that a search result named a sealed field, that a deleted record reappeared from a backup file, or that the app can't tell me the date a record was last changed.

Replying to the "I'd keep my card details in it right away" comment, with respect, because I used to think exactly like that and it's why I'm asking questions.

I also never open settings. That's the problem. On my Mac the "protected vs not protected" choice is a box somebody has to remember to tick, once, months ago, and then never think about again. If I can't see it in the palette, I won't know it, and neither will you. And my situation is worse than yours: the Mac lives in the living room and a teenager uses it. If the vault opens at launch with no prompt, then "unsealed" isn't a settings detail for me — it's the whole question of whether my ID scans and card numbers are sitting there readable behind a screen lock anyone in the house can walk up to.

The "actually make me re-confirm for card numbers even if the item isn't protected" idea is the good part of your comment and I'd go further: for me the default has to be sealed, and you opt OUT. Not "you opt in and hope you remembered." A feature that only protects me if I've been diligent is a feature for organized people, and I'm not one.

Also seconding the audit trail from above. I want to see the list of every time a value was typed and into which window — because "deleted means gone" is what I assumed about everything until I learned otherwise, and I'd rather not find out the hard way again.

Two answers, one of them unwelcome.

For the shared-Mac question above: I would not assume a second macOS account protects you. No cloud sync means the vault is a file on that disk, and if it "opens at launch without a prompt," the only thing between your kid and your records is file permissions and whether the vault key is wrapped to your login keychain or to the Secure Enclave with a user-presence ACL. Those are different products. "Sign out closes the whole vault" is a session statement, not a cryptographic one — if the key material is recoverable from the disk by anyone with the file plus your account, signing out achieves nothing against an admin or a disk image. That's the specific thing I'd want written down before anyone in a shared household stores identity documents here. Test it the unhappy way: second account, try to open the vault file, see what the error actually says.

And for the audit-trail point, which I think is the strongest comment on this thread: a "Saved" badge is a UI confession, not a log. If the app can't tell me what changed and when, it can't tell me whether a sealed field was read by an agent. An export path with no record of what it emitted is precisely the thing that makes sealing cosmetic.

One correction I'd make to my own earlier list, since I said the palette "shows a sealed count": if a locked record is matchable in search at all — by field name, by row count, by a greyed-out result — then it isn't sealed, it's blurred. Sealed should mean absent from search until Touch ID, not present but unusable. Leaking "there is a card here" is metadata an attacker with my search terms doesn't need.

So: threat model document, key hierarchy named, protected items sealed at launch, agent export allowlist enforced in code, and a read/write/export log I can read without a debugger. Give me those four and I'll test the fifth: a restore that actually restores. Until then, my address goes in, my passport doesn't.

To the original poster (comment 3): thank you for being honest about the settings pane, because that's exactly the failure I worry about and it's not really a you problem. "I never open settings" describes about ninety percent of the people I close books with, me included most days. So here's what I'd ask for, and none of it is buried:

- Put the state in the row itself. Every item in the palette shows its last-changed date and whether it's sealed, in the same place I read the name. Not a colour, not an icon I have to learn — words. I'm on a larger-text setting; a badge that shrinks to a dot tells me nothing.
- Make the palette say what it's about to do before it does it. If the top hit is a protected item, the palette should read "sealed — Touch ID to type" instead of typing nothing or, worse, typing something. Right now I can't tell which happened.
- Re-confirm on anything you'd not want in the wrong window. Your card-number idea is the right instinct, but don't tie it to protection status — define it once, in a list I can read, and re-confirm for every field on it.
- Show me the log without asking. A plain list: date, item, field, sealed or not, typed into which app. If a line can't be written, the action shouldn't happen.

That last one is the whole reason I'd hesitate. The app autosaves and shows a "Saved" badge, which tells me a write occurred but not what was written or when or over what. I reconcile accounts for a living; I cannot run my own life on a badge that means "something happened."

To the parent asking about the shared Mac (comment 1): your two questions are the two I'd want answered before anything else, and I'd want the answers as a test, not a promise.

A restore test that would satisfy me, in order: create an item, note its contents and the date it was created; edit it twice and note each date; delete it; quit the app; reopen; search for it. Then restore from whatever backup mechanism exists and confirm the item comes back with both edit dates intact — not just the newest content. If the dates come back missing or reset, then the restore is only cosmetic and I wouldn't trust it with a document I might need to prove something about later. (A card number you can replace. A passport number on a form you filed two years ago, you can't.)

On the shared Mac: the line that matters is "the vault opens at launch without a prompt" together with "sleep and screen lock seal protected items only." That means the unprotected items are sitting decrypted behind your screen lock, every time you walk away. So the honest answer to "what do I have to do every time" is probably: log out of the Mac, not just lock it — and if the app can't tell you that in the main window, you'll forget it by Thursday. Ask for it in writing, and ask what a second account on the same Mac can see with the disk in hand.

I'd also add a third question neither of us can see answered today: what does the app do about backups you make yourself? If there's no cloud sync, and nothing in the UI tells you what a Time Machine copy contains, you may be quietly keeping an old, fully readable copy of the vault on an external drive.

Speaking as a bookkeeper who keeps client records (and as someone who reads every column twice): the "protected = second key + Touch ID" model is good, but it bundles three separate needs — secrecy, session length, and accountability — into one switch. Splitting them:

1) Separate vaults per sensitivity tier instead of one vault with protected items. Helps: anyone who shares a Mac or hands it to a colleague for five minutes. Cost: moderate — two stores, two unlock paths, plus a way to move an item between them (and an undo for that move).

2) Per-field sealing rather than per-item. Helps: anyone whose item is 90% harmless (name, supplier) and 10% sensitive (bank details). Cost: higher — every editor, the palette, and the agent JSON export have to respect field-level state, and a partial record breaks easily when a field list gets reordered.

3) Idle timeout that blanks protected values but keeps the list readable. Helps: the "I stepped away" case. Cost: low-ish, but it needs a visible countdown; a reorder or a silent relock on screen 2 made me lose my place more than once.

4) An explicit "lock everything now" command and a sleep/lock default that seals all items, not just protected ones. Helps: people who expect a vault to behave like a vault. Cost: low. Honestly, "opens at launch without a prompt" is the line that worries me most — I'd want that to be a setting I have to turn off, not the default.

5) An unlock log — when, which item, which fields, whether the agent export ran. Helps: anyone who has to prove who touched a record. Cost: medium, mostly in storage and in a filterable view; note that a log is itself sensitive and must not end up in the agent JSON.

6) Where the agent export is concerned, a hard allow-list per field with a testable "what will print" preview. Helps: anyone wiring automation to bookkeeping data. Cost: medium — but cheaper than one accidental JSON dump.

One cross-cutting note: the "sealed count" badge is the nicest part of the design, because a count is a list that cannot silently reorder. Please keep it visible even when the palette is in large-text mode, and make sure undo survives a relock — autosave plus a sealed field is exactly where a mis-type becomes permanent.

Starting from the unhappy path: "the vault opens at launch without a prompt" means the second key for every protected item is already resident in a process running as me before I've asked for anything. Protected items are then a UI gate, not a crypto boundary — Touch ID gates the *read*, not the key. Anything running as me (a login item, the "agents" command, a debugger, a compromised editor plugin) can walk the whole vault. So I'd start by asking what threat model "protected" is meant to answer, because right now it answers "shoulder-surfer" and nothing else.

Alternatives, roughly by how much they actually move the boundary:

1. Secure Enclave-wrapped per-item key, released on user presence. Enclave holds a P-256 key; per-item data keys are wrapped to it and only unwrapped inside the enclave after biometric auth; plaintext exists only for the duration of the decrypt. Helps against: process-level readers, memory scrapers, an offline copy of the disk. Costs: biometric + enclave entitlements, async round trip on every read (kills the "type the value into the focused field" latency you're relying on), needs a fallback path for machines with no T2/Enclave and for VMs, and you lose bulk plaintext caching so search-over-sealed-fields gets harder.

2. Per-secret Keychain items with kSecAccessControl(.userPresence, .biometryCurrentSet). Cheapest real boundary on macOS, maybe a couple of weeks. Helps: per-secret ACLs, automatic invalidation when enrolled fingerprints change. Costs: Keychain's own pathologies — ACLs tied to signing identity (dev builds "forget" access), migration between Macs is miserable, and prompt fatigue if a single palette action reads forty fields.

3. Split the model: an always-open index plus a sealed body decrypted per read and wiped after. Helps the agent export honestly — you can publish the index without the body, instead of relying on a human's guess about which fields are "non-sensitive." Costs: real schema work to separate indexable metadata from secret material, and Swift will fight you on wiping (ARC, copy-on-write, Foundation caches). Plan for that, not around it.

4. Lock the whole vault on sleep/screen lock, not just protected items — a day's work, mostly edge cases (external displays, clamshell, screen sharing). Helps against the actually common threat: the unlocked laptop on a table. Costs: you'll want a short "unlock for five minutes" lease, which you then have to test the expiry of, including suspend/resume, clock skew, and a user who closes the lid mid-lease.

5. Don't ship the agent JSON export keyed off a *label*. "Marked for agents" makes a security classification out of a checkbox someone ticked once, and the local command then prints with the same privileges as everything else — file perms, same UID, no boundary. Make it per-field opt-in with a visible audit trail of what was exported and when. Costs: audit plumbing and a UI that discourages over-marking.

Also worth stating plainly in the docs: between display wake and the Touch ID prompt, protected fields are sealed; after it, until the next sleep, they're not. That's what people will get wrong.

Replying to comment 1, since I asked myself the same three things and I keep records on a Mac that other people touch.

a) Quit / sign out. The writeup only promises that protected *items* get sealed on sleep and screen lock, and that the whole vault closes on sign-out or quit. That's consistent with what you need, but "closed" needs saying out loud: open again means what — no prompt, or a password? It says the vault opens at launch without a prompt. If that's also true after a quit, then quitting is not a lock; it's just a restart. I'd want that spelled out in one sentence on the box, because "I quit the app" is most people's security plan and it's the wrong one here.

b) Backups. I genuinely don't know, and that's the finding. "No cloud sync" tells me where it isn't. It doesn't tell me whether there's a local backup, whether it's encrypted with the same keys, whether an accidental delete is recoverable, and how long an undo lasts. Until that's answered, I'd copy the vault file myself before I type anything I can't retype — and I'd test the restore on a throwaway item first, not on a client's records.

c) The family Mac is the part I'd worry about most. Same macOS account means, as far as I can tell from the description, the same unlocked vault — no separate records for you and your teenager. Protected items get a Touch ID gate, but the rest of the list and your search history don't. Separate Mac accounts, or separate vaults, would do more for you than any setting here.

On the "no fingerprint prompt for my address" point in the other comment: agreed, and I'd add the reverse. Anything I've marked protected should *stay* protected when the value is typed into a form — check the field after it lands. And the thing I'd ask the developer for: a search that finds a field by whatever name I gave it, not the name the schema prefers. If I label it "phone – work" and the box only matches "telephone," I'll conclude the vault is empty and re-enter it.

@user 3 — taking your questions in order, because they're the right ones and the post above doesn't answer them.

1) "If I quit the app or sign out, does the vault really close?" Quitting does close it: no process, no palette, nothing to type into. But "closed" is not the same as "the data on disk is unreadable by someone else." Any encryption-at-rest scheme has to keep its key somewhere that survives a reboot, and on a Mac that somewhere is normally the login Keychain, unlocked when you log in. So the honest answer is: after quit or sign-out, the app can't read the vault, but another program running as you after you log back in might. Whether that's true for UniversalVault depends entirely on how the second key is stored, and that's the one question I'd ask the developer before trusting it.

2) "Is there a backup?" No cloud sync means no backup. That's a feature and a trap. Time Machine will back up the file, but it will back up whatever key material sits alongside it too, so a restore on another account can bring back a readable vault. Turn on FileVault, keep the backup drive encrypted, and — this matters — test a restore of one record while nothing is at stake. An untested backup is a wish.

3) The family Mac part is the part I'd worry about more than any of this. If your teenager uses the *same* account as you, there is no protection worth the name: same user, same Keychain, same ability to run anything. Separate accounts, teenager not an admin, and your vault in your account only. That one change does more than any Touch ID prompt.

4) Practical test if you want to check it yourself: quit the app, log out, log back in, open Console, and search for the app's process while the vault is shut; then look at whether the vault file is still sitting there with a plausible size. If pressing "quit" silently leaves a helper process or a login item behind, you'll see it. Do it before you put anything in it you'd mind losing.

Small thing on the "Saved" badge while I'm here: autosave plus a sealed field is exactly where a mis-type becomes permanent, so make sure delete/undo survives a relock and isn't part of what gets sealed.
